claims.text: Hold the weight with an underhand (palms-up) grip and rest the forearm on the thigh or on a bench.

quotes.text: Grab a dumbbell with an underhand grip and rest your forearm against your thigh, or alternatively against a bench.
Grab a barbell with an underhand grip and rest your forearms against your thighs, or alternatively against a bench.
While you’re sitting in a chair or on a bench, grasp a barbell or a pair of dumbbells with a supinated grip and rest one forearm on each of your legs.

claims.text: ACE's version kneels with the elbows on a bench, bent about 90 degrees, dumbbells hanging freely off the edge, forearms turned so the palms face up and wrists starting neutral.

quotes.text: Holding two dumbbells, kneel and rest your elbows on a bench with approximately a 90 degree bend at the elbows and the dumbbells hanging freely off the edge of the pad.
Supinate your forearms (rotate the forearms so that the tops are along the bench and the palms are facing upward) keep your wrists in a neutral position (not in flexion or extension).

claims.text: Lower slowly by letting the wrist bend back toward the floor while keeping the grip, without straightening the arms or leaning forward or back, and hold the bottom briefly.

quotes.text: Inhale and slowly allow the wrists to move into extension (allow dumbbells to move towards the floor) without releasing your grip, extending your arms or leaning forward / backward. Hold this end position briefly.

claims.text: Breathe out and slowly curl the wrist up toward you using the forearm flexors to return to the start.

quotes.text: Exhale and slowly contract your forearm flexor muscles (along the top of the forearm) rolling your wrists towards you in order to return the dumbbells back to the starting position.

claims.text: People sometimes loosen the grip and let the dumbbell roll to the fingertips on the way down; ACE says this raises the risk of wrist injury and of dropping the weight, and advises squeezing hard in both phases. Three of the four technique sources say the opposite: StrengthLog's dumbbell and barbell pages tell lifters to let the weight roll out into the fingers, and BarBend to let the handle glide down into the fingertips. ACE is the only read source that ties the roll to harm, so the closed grip stays the shown line (LR-18, R-LB5-3).

quotes.text: Individuals sometimes release their grip during the lowering phase, allowing the dumbbells to roll towards their finger tips. While this may increase the load on the forearm muscles, it also increases the risk of wrist injury and dropping the dumbbells.
To increase strength think about squeezing the weights as hard as possible during both phases of the movement.
Lower your hand towards the floor, and let the dumbbell roll out in your fingers.
So, when you’re performing wrist curling motions in particular, allow the handle of the weight to glide down into your fingertips and then curl it back into the base of your palm as you contract.
Lower your hands towards the floor, and let the barbell roll out in your fingers.

claims.text: With the hands hanging over an edge the wrists are in a vulnerable position, so keep the weight light and use higher reps (about 15-20).

quotes.text: As with kneeling wrist curls, the fact that your hands hang over a solid edge places them in a somewhat precarious position. Lighter weights are advised here and in a rep range of 15 to 20

claims.text: Progress by adding reps or cutting rest rather than adding weight in most cases.

quotes.text: aim for amping up your rep count or reducing rest times rather than working with a heavier weight in most cases.

claims.text: The wrist curl trains the forearm muscles that bend the wrist and close the hand (the forearm flexors).

quotes.text: Dumbbell wrist curls train the muscles in the forearm that flexes (bends) the wrist and closes your hand.
Primary muscles worked: Forearm Flexors

claims.text: Resting the forearms on a support keeps the biceps from taking over, so the forearms do the work.

quotes.text: By resting your forearms on a weight bench, your biceps will be thoroughly unable to take over the exercise.

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting, down = lowering): a slow 2 s up and 2 s down, the slow end of ACSM's moderate 1-2 s each way, which is stated for advanced training (LR-15); ACE asks for slow movement both ways and BarBend for a slow and controlled tempo, with no seconds. ACE's brief hold is at the bottom, after the lowering, with no seconds; no quote asks for a pause right after the curl up.

aiming for a slow and controlled tempo to bolster your time under tension.
at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

plate.viewWhy: The wrist bends up and down in the side plane with the forearm lying still on its support (c1, c3), so it reads side-on; the census notes the wrist travel is small and needs a zoomed camera or the hand close-up.
plate.equipment: Flat bench to sit on (census); one dumbbell (c1).
plate.start: Seated, forearm resting on the thigh (c1) with the hand hanging freely past the knee (hang-off-the-edge from ACE's bench version, c2); palm up, closed grip, wrist neutral (c1, c2, c5).
plate.end: Wrist curled up toward the forearm, grip still closed (c4, c5); forearm still on the thigh, arms not extending, torso not leaning (c1, c3).

mistake.what: Arms extending or body leaning forward to move the weight.
mistake.why: The fault ACE names, the grip opening so the dumbbell rolls to the fingertips (c5), raises the risk of wrist injury and of dropping the weight but needs fingers the engine does not draw (fist circle), so it is shown in the hand zoom; ACE's lowering step rules out extending the arms or leaning (c3), which shows side-on.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: loosening the grip so the dumbbell rolls to the fingertips (c5). Step 1 set aside: ACE's "Individuals sometimes release their grip during the lowering phase" uses 'sometimes', which is not a frequency word; BarBend's "Most wrist curl variations neglect radial and ulnar deviation", "common in many sports", "Many of the muscles in your wrist and forearm also control your fingers", "in most cases" and "In the overwhelming majority of cases" are about exercises, muscles, progression and scheduling. Step 2: the grip release is the only named fault a quote ties to harm: "it also increases the risk of wrist injury and dropping the dumbbells" (ACE, c5). Set aside: BarBend's "places them in a somewhat precarious position" (c6) is about hands over an edge, a setup, and the heavy-weight item is a load choice; "less risky" and "safely" are about other variations. Three of the four technique sources let the weight roll: StrengthLog's dumbbell page ("let the dumbbell roll out in your fingers"), StrengthLog's barbell page ("Lower your hands towards the floor, and let the barbell roll out in your fingers.") and BarBend ("allow the handle of the weight to glide down into your fingertips"), all c5. ACE is the only read source that ties the roll to harm, so the card keeps ACE's harm-linked fault and the closed grip stays the shown line (LR-18, R-LB5-3). drawable is false: the fault needs open fingers, which the engine does not draw (fist circle), so it is shown in the hand zoom, handlingMistakes[0] stays the grip release, and plate.mistake names the next fault by the same steps. Step 2 has no other candidate. Step 3: no read source has a common-mistakes list, so the fault the most read sources tell the lifter to avoid: extending the arms or leaning forward or back (ACE, c3), the only other fault a source says to avoid; it reads side-on. Pick unchanged.

tells.text: Fist stays closed all the way

tempo.text: Pause 0 (LR-33): ACE's "Hold this end position briefly." ends the downward phase, so the hold is at the bottom with the wrist bent back, not right after the curl up, and it gives no seconds. No quote on the card asks for a pause after the curl up. Up 2 and down 2 rest on ACSM's 1-2 s (stated for advanced training, WEAK, LR-15) at its slow end, with ACE's "slowly" in both phases and BarBend's "slow and controlled tempo".

plate.variantLine: Drawn seated with one dumbbell, forearm on the thigh (StrengthLog, c1). The barbell version (c1) and ACE's kneeling version on a bench (c2) share the grip, lowering and grip-closed lines (c3, c4, c5).
